goals: Describe the phases of the cell cycle and the events of G1, S, G2 and M
Describe the stages of mitosis and cytokinesis in animal and plant cells

slides.heading: Cell Cycle and Cell Division
slides.body_md: Part 1 — how a cell prepares for division and how mitosis shares out its chromosomes.

nodes.label: Cell grows and copies its DNA

visual.alt: Flow from a growing cell through mitosis and cytokinesis to two daughter cells

slides.narration: Every cell comes from a pre-existing cell. A cell grows, copies its genetic material, and then divides into two. In this part we follow one turn of the cell cycle, and then watch in detail how the chromosomes are shared out during mitosis.

slides.heading: The cell cycle
slides.body_md: The **cell cycle** is the sequence of events by which a cell duplicates its genome, synthesises other constituents and divides into two daughter cells. It has two parts: **interphase** and the **M phase** (mitosis).

slides.narration: Human cells in culture take about twenty four hours for one cycle, while yeast needs only about ninety minutes. The actual division, the M phase, is the shortest part. The long interphase, which lies between two M phases, is when the cell prepares: it is anything but a resting phase.

slides.heading: Interphase: G one, S and G two
slides.body_md: **Interphase** is the time between two M phases. Cell growth and DNA replication happen in an orderly sequence.

rows: Cell is metabolically active and grows; no DNA replication
DNA replicates; in animal cells the centriole duplicates in the cytoplasm
DNA rises from 2C to 4C; chromosome number stays 2n
Proteins for mitosis are made; growth continues

visual.alt: Table of the events of G1, S and G2 with DNA content and chromosome number

slides.narration: In the first gap phase the cell grows and is metabolically active, but does not copy its DNA. In S phase the DNA is replicated, so the amount doubles, although the number of chromosomes does not change. In animal cells the centriole also duplicates in the cytoplasm. In the second gap phase proteins for mitosis are made and growth goes on.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: the arithmetic of the cycle
slides.body_md: Human cells in culture take about 24 hours per cycle, with the M phase lasting about 1 hour. Yeast divides about once in 90 minutes. (a) What share of the human cycle is interphase? (b) How many yeast cells arise from one cell in 9 hours?
bullets: Interphase lasts $24 - 1 = 23$ hours, so its share is $\dfrac{23}{24} \times 100 \approx 95.8$ percent.
In 9 hours, which is $540$ minutes, there are $\dfrac{540}{90} = 6$ cycles.
Each cycle doubles the number: $2^{6} = 64$ cells.

visual.alt: Worked table: interphase about 95.8 percent; 64 yeast cells after nine hours

slides.narration: Twenty three of the twenty four hours are interphase, so it makes up nearly ninety six percent of the cycle. Nine hours is five hundred and forty minutes, which is six ninety minute cycles. Each cycle doubles the number of cells, so one yeast cell becomes sixty four.

slides.narration: In first gap phase the nucleus has the basic amount of DNA, called two C. During S phase it rises steadily to four C and stays there through the second gap phase and mitosis. When the cell divides, each daughter nucleus gets two C again. Replication adds chromatids, not new chromosomes.

slides.heading: G zero: the quiescent stage
slides.body_md: Some cells leave G1 and enter **G0**, the **quiescent stage**: the cell is **metabolically active but no longer proliferates** unless called on to do so. Many cells of the adult body, such as heart cells, stay in G0; others re-enter the cycle when needed.

rows: Remain in G0 and do not divide
Divide repeatedly through life, so they cycle continuously
Leave G0 and divide when repair is needed

visual.alt: Table of cell types showing G0, continuous cycling and re-entry into the cycle

slides.narration: A cell that stops dividing leaves the cycle at first gap phase and enters the quiescent stage. It stays alive and active. Heart cells are an example. Some quiescent cells can be called back into the cycle, for instance when a wound needs repair.

slides.heading: Mitosis: the stages
slides.body_md: **Mitosis** is an **equational division**: the daughter cells receive the same chromosome number as the parent. It has two parts: **karyokinesis** (division of the nucleus) and **cytokinesis** (division of the cytoplasm).

slides.narration: Prophase begins with the condensation of chromosomes, each already made of two chromatids joined at the centromere. The centrosomes move to opposite poles. Late in prophase the nuclear envelope, nucleolus, Golgi complex and endoplasmic reticulum disappear. Mitosis is a continuous process, and we divide it into stages only for convenience.

slides.heading: Metaphase and anaphase
slides.body_md: In **metaphase** the chromosomes are fully condensed and **spindle fibres attach to the kinetochores** of each chromosome. They lie on the **metaphase plate**. In **anaphase** the **centromeres split** and the chromatids move **centromere first** to opposite poles.

rows: Chromosomes aligned at the equator; one chromatid of each chromosome attached to each pole
Best stage to count chromosomes and study their shape
Centromeres split; chromatids, now chromosomes, move to opposite poles
Each pole receives a complete set of chromosomes

visual.alt: Table comparing metaphase and anaphase of mitosis

slides.narration: At metaphase the chromosomes are at their most condensed, which makes this the best stage for counting them and studying their shape. Spindle fibres from opposite poles hold the two chromatids of each chromosome. At anaphase the centromeres split, and each chromatid, now a chromosome, is pulled to a pole, centromere leading.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: reading a mitotic index
slides.body_md: A student counts 400 cells in a stained root-tip squash: 352 in interphase, 24 in prophase, 8 in metaphase, 4 in anaphase and 12 in telophase. The cell cycle of these cells lasts 20 hours. Find the mitotic index and the time spent in metaphase.
bullets: Dividing cells: $24 + 8 + 4 + 12 = 48$.
Mitotic index: $\dfrac{48}{400} \times 100 = 12$ percent.
Metaphase time: $\dfrac{8}{400} \times 20 = 0.4$ hour, which is $24$ minutes.

visual.alt: Worked table: mitotic index 12 percent; metaphase lasts 24 minutes

slides.narration: Forty eight of four hundred cells are dividing, a mitotic index of twelve percent. In a population where cells are at all stages, the share of cells in a phase matches the share of time the phase lasts. Eight out of four hundred is two percent of twenty hours, which is twenty four minutes of metaphase.

slides.heading: Significance of mitosis
slides.body_md: Mitosis produces **genetically identical** daughter cells with the **same chromosome number**.

rows: A zygote becomes a multicellular body; cell number rises
A growing cell divides when its cytoplasm outgrows the control of its nucleus
Cells of the skin and the lining of the intestine; wound healing
Meristematic tissues divide throughout life, forming new cells at root and shoot tips

visual.alt: Table of the roles of mitosis with examples

slides.narration: Because each daughter cell receives an exact copy of the parental chromosomes, mitosis keeps the genetic make up constant. It is the basis of growth. It restores the balance between the nucleus and the cytoplasm of a growing cell, replaces worn out cells, and in plants keeps the meristems producing new cells all through life.

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: The cell cycle has a long interphase (G1, S, G2) and a short M phase.
DNA replicates in S phase: 2C becomes 4C, chromosomes stay 2n.
G0 is the quiescent stage; cells may re-enter the cycle.
Mitosis stages: prophase, metaphase, anaphase, telophase; then cytokinesis.
Animal cells divide by a furrow; plant cells by a cell plate.
Mitosis gives identical cells: growth, repair and replacement.

slides.heading: Meiosis
slides.body_md: Part 2 — the reduction division that makes gametes and keeps the chromosome number constant.

visual.alt: Flow from a diploid meiocyte through meiosis I and II to four haploid cells

slides.narration: Sexual reproduction joins two gametes. If gametes were diploid, the chromosome number would double in every generation. Meiosis prevents this by halving the number. It takes place in specialised diploid cells, called meiocytes, to form gametes or spores.

slides.heading: What happens in meiosis
slides.body_md: **Meiosis** involves **two sequential cycles of nuclear and cell division**, meiosis I and meiosis II, but only a **single cycle of DNA replication**. It produces **four haploid cells**.

rows: A diploid meiocyte after S phase
Two: meiosis I (reduction) and meiosis II (equational)

visual.alt: Table of the main features of meiosis

slides.narration: The DNA is copied only once, but the nucleus divides twice. In meiosis I the homologous chromosomes are separated, which halves the chromosome number. Meiosis II then separates the sister chromatids, much like mitosis. The result is four haploid cells.

slides.heading: Prophase I: five substages
slides.body_md: Prophase I is **much longer and more complex** than mitotic prophase. It is divided into **leptotene, zygotene, pachytene, diplotene and diakinesis**.

slides.narration: In leptotene the chromosomes begin to condense and become visible. In zygotene homologous chromosomes pair up, which is called synapsis. In pachytene the pairs are seen as tetrads of four chromatids, and crossing over takes place. In diplotene the homologues start to separate but stay joined at chiasmata. In diakinesis the chiasmata move to the ends, and the envelope breaks down.

slides.heading: Prophase I in more detail
slides.body_md: Learn each substage by its **signature event**.

rows: Chromosomes become gradually visible under the light microscope; compaction continues
Homologues pair (**synapsis**); the paired chromosomes are **bivalents**, held by the **synaptonemal complex**
Bivalent shows four chromatids, a **tetrad**; **crossing over** at recombination nodules, catalysed by the enzyme recombinase
Synaptonemal complex dissolves; homologues separate but remain held at **chiasmata**, the sites of crossing over
Chiasmata **terminalise**; chromosomes fully condensed; meiotic spindle assembles; nucleolus and nuclear envelope disappear

visual.alt: Table of the five substages of prophase I with their signature events

slides.narration: Crossing over is the exchange of genetic material between non-sister chromatids of homologous chromosomes. It happens in pachytene and gives recombination. The X shaped chiasmata are visible in diplotene. By the end of diakinesis the cell is ready for the first division, with the spindle assembled and the nuclear envelope gone.

slides.body_md: After prophase I: **metaphase I**, **anaphase I** and **telophase I** make meiosis I; then **prophase II, metaphase II, anaphase II and telophase II** make meiosis II.

slides.narration: In the picture, the top row is meiosis I and the bottom row meiosis II. Tips of swapped colour show where crossing over happened. Notice that meiosis I separates whole chromosomes of a pair, while meiosis II separates chromatids. After telophase two, four haploid cells are present.

slides.heading: Meiosis I: metaphase to telophase
slides.body_md: In **metaphase I** the **bivalents** align on the equatorial plate, with the kinetochores of each homologue attached to one pole. In **anaphase I** the **homologous chromosomes separate**, but the **sister chromatids stay together** at the centromeres.

rows: Bivalent chromosomes align on the equatorial plate; microtubules from opposite poles attach to the kinetochores of homologous chromosomes
Homologous chromosomes separate; chromatids remain associated at their centromeres
Nuclear membrane and nucleolus reappear; cytokinesis gives a **dyad** of cells
Short stage between the two divisions; **no DNA replication**

visual.alt: Table of metaphase I, anaphase I, telophase I and interkinesis

slides.narration: In anaphase one whole homologous chromosomes move apart, so each pole receives half the chromosome number, though each chromosome still has two chromatids. Cytokinesis gives a dyad of two cells. A short stage, interkinesis, follows. There is no DNA replication in it, and the chromosomes are not copied again.

slides.heading: Meiosis II
slides.body_md: Meiosis II resembles a mitotic division in each of the two cells of the dyad, but the cells are **haploid**.

rows: Nuclear membrane disappears; chromosomes become compact again
Chromosomes align at the equator; kinetochores of sister chromatids attach to spindle fibres from opposite poles
Centromere splits; chromatids move to opposite poles
Two groups of chromosomes enclosed by nuclear envelopes; cytokinesis gives a **tetrad** of four haploid cells

visual.alt: Table of the four stages of meiosis II

slides.narration: The second division goes on in both cells of the dyad at once. Chromosomes line up, the centromeres split, and the sister chromatids separate. Nuclear envelopes form around each group, and cytokinesis completes a tetrad of four haploid cells.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: counting through meiosis
slides.body_md: A pea plant has 2n = 14 chromosomes. Count the chromosomes and chromatids at each stage of meiosis in one meiocyte, and the number of bivalents.
bullets: Bivalents: $\dfrac{14}{2} = 7$. At prophase I there are $14$ chromosomes with $2 \times 14 = 28$ chromatids.
Anaphase I: $7$ chromosomes ($14$ chromatids) go to each pole, so each cell of the dyad has $7$ chromosomes.
Anaphase II: the centromeres split, so each cell momentarily has $14$ chromosomes; each final cell has $7$.

visual.alt: Table of chromosome and chromatid numbers through meiosis in a pea cell with fourteen chromosomes

slides.narration: Fourteen chromosomes make seven bivalents. At prophase one there are fourteen chromosomes, each of two chromatids, so twenty eight chromatids. Anaphase one sends seven chromosomes to each pole. In anaphase two the centromeres split, and each cell briefly has fourteen chromosomes; each final cell has seven.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: DNA and gametes
slides.body_md: The nucleus of a certain plant holds 9.6 pg of DNA in G1. Find the DNA per nucleus after S phase, after meiosis I and after meiosis II. How many pollen grains come from 250 pollen mother cells?
bullets: After S phase the DNA doubles: $2 \times 9.6 = 19.2$ pg.
Meiosis I halves it: $\dfrac{19.2}{2} = 9.6$ pg per cell, with half the chromosomes, each of two chromatids.
Meiosis II halves it again: $\dfrac{9.6}{2} = 4.8$ pg per cell. Each pollen mother cell gives 4 pollen grains, so $4 \times 250 = 1000$.

visual.alt: Worked table: DNA 9.6, 19.2, 9.6 and 4.8 picograms; 1000 pollen grains from 250 meiocytes

slides.narration: DNA doubles in S phase, is halved at the first division, and halved again at the second, so each gamete has half the DNA of a first gap phase nucleus. One meiocyte gives four haploid cells, so two hundred and fifty pollen mother cells give one thousand pollen grains.

slides.heading: Mitosis and meiosis compared
slides.body_md: Know the **differences** clearly: they are a favourite long-answer topic.

rows: Two, diploid, identical to the parent

visual.alt: Table comparing mitosis and meiosis

slides.narration: Mitosis makes two identical diploid cells for growth and repair. Meiosis makes four haploid cells that differ from one another and from the parent. Only in meiosis do homologous chromosomes pair and exchange segments, and only in meiosis is there one replication for two divisions.

slides.heading: Significance of meiosis
slides.body_md: Meiosis **conserves the chromosome number** from one generation to the next in sexually reproducing organisms, and **increases genetic variability**, which is vital for evolution.

rows: Fusion of two haploid gametes restores the diploid number
New combinations of genes on a chromosome (recombination)
Separation of homologues in anaphase I
Different mixes of maternal and paternal chromosomes in the gametes

visual.alt: Table of how meiosis maintains chromosome number and creates variation

slides.narration: Without meiosis the chromosome number would double each generation. Meiosis halves it so that fertilisation restores it. Crossing over and the separation of homologues give gametes with new combinations of genes. This variation in a population is important for the process of evolution.

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: Meiosis: one DNA replication, two divisions, four haploid cells.
Prophase I: leptotene, zygotene (synapsis), pachytene (crossing over), diplotene (chiasmata), diakinesis (terminalisation).
Anaphase I separates homologues; anaphase II separates chromatids.
Interkinesis has no DNA replication.
Meiosis keeps the chromosome number constant and creates variation.

sections.heading: 1. The cell cycle
sections.body_md:
All cells reproduce by dividing: a cell grows, duplicates its genome, synthesises other constituents and divides into two daughter cells. This sequence of events is the **cell cycle**. The duration varies with the organism and cell type: **human cells in culture take about 24 hours**, of which the **M phase lasts only about 1 hour**, whereas **yeast** completes a cycle in about **90 minutes**.

The cycle has two parts. **M phase (mitosis phase)** is the actual division; **interphase** lies between two successive M phases and, in human cells, is more than **95 percent** of the cycle (95.8 percent for the textbook figures). Interphase is a period of preparation, not a resting phase:
- **G1 phase (gap 1):** between the end of mitosis and the start of DNA replication; the cell is metabolically active and grows but does **not replicate its DNA**.
- **S phase (synthesis):** DNA **replicates**; the amount per cell **doubles** (from 2C to 4C) but the **chromosome number remains the same** (2n). In animal cells the **centriole duplicates in the cytoplasm** during S phase.
- **G2 phase (gap 2):** proteins are synthesised in preparation for mitosis, and cell growth continues.

Some cells do not divide further: they exit G1 and enter an inactive **quiescent stage (G0)**. Cells in G0 remain metabolically active but do not proliferate unless called on to do so by the needs of the organism; many cells of the adult body, such as heart cells, stay in this stage, while others re-enter the cycle.

(The textbook figures of 24 hours and 90 minutes are typical values for cells in culture; real cycle times vary widely, and the phase lengths drawn in the diagrams are illustrative.)

sections.heading: 2. Mitosis
sections.body_md:
**Mitosis** is the division in which a **diploid parent cell gives two daughter cells with the same chromosome number**, so it is called **equational division**. It is a continuous process, divided into **karyokinesis** (division of the nucleus) and **cytokinesis** (division of the cytoplasm), and karyokinesis is described in four stages.

- **Prophase** follows the S and G2 phases. Chromosomal material, which was a tangle of thin threads in interphase, **condenses**; each chromosome has two **chromatids** joined at the **centromere**. The **centrosome**, duplicated in S phase, begins to move to opposite poles and radiates **microtubules**, the **asters**; the two asters with the spindle fibres form the **mitotic apparatus**. By the **end of prophase**, the **Golgi complex, endoplasmic reticulum, nucleolus and nuclear envelope disappear**.
- **Metaphase:** the chromosomes are fully condensed and **spindle fibres attach to the kinetochores** (disc-shaped structures at the centromere). The chromosomes **align at the equator, the metaphase plate**; one chromatid of each chromosome is connected to a pole by spindle fibres, the other to the opposite pole. Metaphase is the **best stage to count and study chromosome morphology**.
- **Anaphase:** the **centromeres split** and the chromatids **separate**; each, now a chromosome, **moves to the opposite pole**, **centromere first**.
- **Telophase:** the chromosomes **reach the poles** and **decondense**; the **nuclear envelope reforms** around each group, and the **nucleolus, Golgi complex and ER reform**.

**Cytokinesis** follows. In an **animal cell** a **furrow** appears in the plasma membrane and deepens until the cell is divided. In a **plant cell**, which has a rigid wall, a **cell plate** forms in the centre and grows outwards to meet the side walls; it represents the **middle lamella** between the new cells, and the cell wall materials are then laid down on it. Sometimes karyokinesis is **not followed by cytokinesis**, giving **multinucleate** cells (**syncytium**), as in the **liquid endosperm of coconut**.

**Significance:** daughter cells are genetically identical to the parent, so mitosis maintains the genetic make-up. It is responsible for **growth** (the zygote becomes a multicellular body), it **restores the nucleo-cytoplasmic ratio** when a growing cell becomes too large for its nucleus, it **replaces and repairs** cells (skin, intestinal lining) and, in plants, it enables the **meristems** to add new cells throughout life.

**Counting:** a diploid cell with 2n = 8 has 8 chromosomes (16 chromatids) at metaphase; at anaphase, once the centromeres split, the whole cell holds 16 chromosomes, and each daughter nucleus ends up with 8. The **mitotic index** is the percentage of cells in division in a sample, and in a population with cells at all stages the share of cells in a stage is proportional to the time spent in it.

sections.heading: 3. Meiosis
sections.body_md:
**Meiosis** is the specialised division that produces **haploid gametes** from **diploid meiocytes** (gamete mother cells) so that the chromosome number stays constant across generations. It involves **two sequential cycles of nuclear and cell division, meiosis I and meiosis II, but only a single cycle of DNA replication**. Meiosis I is initiated after the parental chromosomes have replicated to produce identical sister chromatids at the S phase. Meiosis I is the **reduction division**; meiosis II is **equational**. Four haploid cells result.

**Meiosis I — prophase I** is prolonged and has five substages.
- **Leptotene:** chromosomes gradually become visible under the light microscope; compaction continues.
- **Zygotene:** homologous chromosomes start pairing and aligning (**synapsis**), aided by the **synaptonemal complex**. The paired chromosomes are called **bivalents** or **tetrads**.
- **Pachytene:** the bivalents clearly appear as tetrads of four chromatids. **Crossing over**, the exchange of segments between **non-sister chromatids** of homologous chromosomes, occurs at **recombination nodules**, and is catalysed by the enzyme **recombinase**.
- **Diplotene:** dissolution of the synaptonemal complex; the recombined homologous chromosomes separate except at the sites of crossovers, the **X-shaped chiasmata**. In oocytes of some vertebrates diplotene can last for months or years.
- **Diakinesis:** **terminalisation of chiasmata**; chromosomes are fully condensed and the **meiotic spindle is assembled**; the **nucleolus disappears and the nuclear envelope breaks down**, marking the end of prophase I.

**Metaphase I:** the bivalents **align on the equatorial plate**; microtubules from opposite poles attach to the **kinetochores of the homologous chromosomes**. **Anaphase I:** the **homologous chromosomes separate**, while **sister chromatids remain associated at their centromeres**. **Telophase I:** the nuclear membrane and nucleolus reappear; **cytokinesis** follows and the product is a **dyad** of cells. The stage between the two meiotic divisions is **interkinesis**; it is generally short-lived and **no DNA replication occurs**.

**Meiosis II — prophase II:** the nuclear membrane disappears and the chromosomes become compact again. **Metaphase II:** the chromosomes align at the equator, and the kinetochores of sister chromatids attach to spindle fibres from opposite poles. **Anaphase II:** the **centromere splits** and the **chromatids move to opposite poles**. **Telophase II:** two groups of chromosomes are enclosed by nuclear envelopes; **cytokinesis** gives a **tetrad** of four **haploid** cells.

**Counting.** For 2n = 14: there are 7 bivalents; a cell of the dyad has 7 chromosomes of two chromatids each; at anaphase II each cell momentarily has 14 chromosomes; each final cell has 7. If the G1 nucleus has 9.6 pg of DNA, it has 19.2 pg after S, 9.6 pg per cell after meiosis I (half the chromosomes, still two chromatids each) and 4.8 pg after meiosis II.

**Significance:** meiosis **conserves the chromosome number** from generation to generation in sexually reproducing organisms (fusion of two haploid gametes restores the diploid number), and it **increases genetic variability** through crossing over and the separation of homologues; variations are very important for evolution.

key_terms.definition_md: A diploid cell of the reproductive organ that undergoes meiosis.
Pairing of homologous chromosomes in zygotene.
Exchange of segments between non-sister chromatids of homologous chromosomes in pachytene.
X-shaped point where homologues remain joined in diplotene, marking a crossover.
The two cells formed after meiosis I, and the four haploid cells formed after meiosis II.
Short stage between meiosis I and meiosis II with no DNA replication.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Writing that chromosome number doubles in S phase (the DNA content doubles; the number of chromosomes stays 2n).
- Calling anaphase the stage when chromosomes align (that is metaphase), or placing the nuclear envelope's disappearance in telophase.
- Saying a plant cell divides by a furrow, or an animal cell by a cell plate.
- Mixing the order of the prophase I substages, or placing crossing over in zygotene (it is in pachytene).
- Saying sister chromatids separate in anaphase I (homologous chromosomes separate; chromatids separate in anaphase II).
- Claiming DNA is replicated in interkinesis, or that cells after meiosis I have C amount of DNA (it is still 2C).

**How marks are usually awarded**
- 1-mark items: a phase or substage name, a chromosome count, a term such as chiasma, dyad or kinetochore, an assertion-reason on S phase or anaphase I.
- 2–3-mark answers: events of G1, S and G2; differences between animal and plant cytokinesis; significance of mitosis or meiosis; events of anaphase I and II; the five substages of prophase I.
- 5-mark answers: stages of mitosis; stages of meiosis I with a labelled diagram; mitosis versus meiosis.
- Numericals: mitotic index, time in a phase from cell counts, cell numbers after n cycles, chromosomes and chromatids at a stage, DNA at a stage — always show the working.

cards.back_md: The sequence of events by which a cell duplicates its genome, makes other constituents and divides into two cells.

cards.front_md: The two parts of the cell cycle?
cards.back_md: Interphase (G1, S, G2) and M phase (mitosis).

cards.front_md: Typical cycle times of human cells in culture and of yeast?
cards.back_md: About 24 hours (M phase about 1 hour); yeast about 90 minutes.
Cell grows and is metabolically active; no DNA replication.
DNA replicates (2C to 4C); chromosome number stays 2n; centriole duplicates in animal cells.
Proteins for mitosis are made; growth continues.
The quiescent stage: cells are metabolically active but do not divide unless called on.

cards.front_md: Share of the cycle taken by interphase in human cells?
cards.back_md: More than 95 percent.

cards.front_md: DNA content and chromosome number from G1 to G2?
cards.back_md: DNA doubles (2C to 4C); chromosome number unchanged (2n).
Cells in M phase divided by total cells counted, times 100.

cards.front_md: Why is mitosis called equational division?
cards.back_md: Daughter cells have the same chromosome number as the parent.
Karyokinesis is division of the nucleus; cytokinesis is division of the cytoplasm.

cards.front_md: What happens in prophase of mitosis?
cards.back_md: Chromosomes condense; centrosomes move to poles; at the end the nuclear envelope, nucleolus, Golgi and ER disappear.
Metaphase.
The equatorial plane on which the chromosomes align.

cards.front_md: What attaches spindle fibres to a chromosome?
cards.back_md: The kinetochore at the centromere.
Centromeres split; chromatids move to opposite poles, centromere first.
Chromosomes decondense at the poles; nuclear envelope, nucleolus, Golgi and ER reform.
Animal: furrow from the edge inwards. Plant: cell plate from the centre outwards.
The middle lamella between the two new plant cells.
When karyokinesis is not followed by cytokinesis, as in coconut liquid endosperm.
Growth, nucleo-cytoplasmic ratio, repair and replacement, meristem activity.

cards.front_md: How many DNA replications and divisions in meiosis?
cards.back_md: One replication, two divisions; four haploid cells.

cards.front_md: The five substages of prophase I in order?
cards.back_md: Leptotene, zygotene, pachytene, diplotene, diakinesis.

cards.front_md: What is synapsis, and when does it happen?
cards.back_md: Pairing of homologous chromosomes, in zygotene, with the synaptonemal complex.

cards.front_md: Where and how does crossing over occur?
cards.back_md: Pachytene; between non-sister chromatids, at recombination nodules, with recombinase.
X-shaped sites of crossing over where homologues remain joined in diplotene.

cards.front_md: What separates in anaphase I and in anaphase II?
cards.back_md: Anaphase I: homologous chromosomes. Anaphase II: sister chromatids.
The short stage between meiosis I and II; no DNA replication.
Keeps chromosome number constant across generations; increases genetic variability.

questions.stem_md: A time-lapse film of cultured cells shows each cell sitting quietly and slowly enlarging for hours, with only a brief burst of visible chromosome movement before it splits in two. What is a cell doing during the long quiet hours?

options.text_md: It is metabolically active: growing and preparing for division, including copying its DNA
It is completely inactive and waits for the M phase
It is carrying out karyokinesis very slowly
It is dividing its cytoplasm gradually

questions.solution_md: The quiet period is interphase (G1, S and G2): the cell grows, replicates its DNA and makes proteins for mitosis, so it is far from resting — option (a).

questions.stem_md: A researcher gives a culture a radioactive building block of DNA for ten minutes, then washes it away. Afterwards, the nuclei of only some of the cells are found to be labelled. The labelled cells had been in

options.text_md: G1 phase, when the cell was growing
G2 phase, when proteins for mitosis were made
M phase, when the chromosomes were separating
S phase, when DNA was being replicated

questions.solution_md: Only cells that were copying DNA during the ten minutes could take in the label; DNA replication is the event of S phase — option (d).

questions.stem_md: A drug stops cells from making the proteins needed to build the spindle. Treated cells finish DNA replication normally but never begin mitosis. In which phase will they be held?
questions.solution_md: Proteins for mitosis are made in G2, after S phase and before the M phase; with the S phase complete and mitosis not started, the cells are held in G2 — option (a).

questions.stem_md: A mature heart muscle cell stays alive and metabolically active for decades without dividing. This state is best described as

options.text_md: a quiescent stage, G0, entered by leaving G1

questions.solution_md: Cells that do not divide further exit G1 for the quiescent stage G0, in which they remain metabolically active — option (a).

questions.stem_md: A cell has 9.6 pg of DNA in its G1 nucleus and 2n = 16. Which description fits the nucleus of the same cell in G2?
questions.solution_md: S phase doubles the DNA (9.6 to 19.2 pg) by making sister chromatids, but each pair of chromatids stays joined at one centromere, so the chromosome number is still 16 — option (c).

questions.stem_md: Measurements on a cell line show DNA per nucleus rising from 2C to 4C over 8 hours, staying at 4C for 5 more hours, then falling to 2C in each daughter cell. The 5-hour plateau at 4C is made up of

options.text_md: G1 phase and the M phase
G2 phase and the M phase

questions.solution_md: The rise is S phase. DNA stays at 4C through G2 and through mitosis, and falls only when the cell divides at the end of the M phase — option (d).

questions.stem_md: During which part of the cell cycle of an animal cell does the centriole duplicate, and where?

options.text_md: In G1 phase, inside the nucleus
In S phase, in the cytoplasm

questions.solution_md: While DNA replicates in the nucleus during S phase, the centriole duplicates in the cytoplasm — option (c).

questions.stem_md: True or false? During S phase the number of chromosomes in a nucleus doubles, from 2n to 4n.
questions.solution_md: False. DNA content doubles (2C to 4C) but the sister chromatids stay joined at one centromere, so the number of chromosomes stays 2n.

questions.stem_md: The phase of the cell cycle between the end of mitosis and the start of DNA replication is called the ______ phase.
questions.solution_md: G1 (gap 1).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The chromosome number of a G2 nucleus is the same as that of the G1 nucleus of the same cell.

**Reason (R):** In most cells the interphase lasts much longer than the M phase.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: Both statements are true, but the length of interphase does not explain the chromosome number: it stays 2n because the sister chromatids remain joined at one centromere — option (b).

questions.stem_md: The root-tip cells of a seedling each divide once every 12 hours. Starting from one cell, and assuming every cell keeps dividing, how many cells will there be after 3 days?
questions.solution_md: 3 days $= 72$ hours, so $\dfrac{72}{12} = 6$ cycles, and $2^{6} = 64$ cells.

questions.stem_md: A fertilised egg divides by mitosis and every cell divides at the same rate. How many rounds of mitosis are needed to make an embryo of 256 cells?
questions.solution_md: Cells double each round: $2^{n} = 256$, so $n = 8$ rounds.

questions.stem_md: A culture whose cells are all at different stages has a cell cycle of 16 hours. In a count of 1200 cells, 450 are found to be in S phase. How many hours does S phase last?
questions.solution_md: The share of cells in a phase equals the share of the cycle spent in it: $\dfrac{450}{1200} \times 16 = 6$ hours.

marking_scheme.step: Share of cells equals share of time

questions.stem_md: A cell line has a cycle of 18 hours, of which the M phase lasts 45 minutes. What percentage of the cycle is interphase? (Answer to one decimal place.)
questions.solution_md: M phase $= 0.75$ h, so interphase $= 18 - 0.75 = 17.25$ h and $\dfrac{17.25}{18} \times 100 = 95.8$ percent (to one decimal place).

questions.stem_md: Name the three phases of interphase and state one event that takes place in each.

answer.model_answer_md: **G1:** the cell grows and is metabolically active, but does not replicate its DNA. **S:** DNA is replicated, so its amount doubles (the chromosome number stays the same), and the centriole duplicates in animal cells. **G2:** proteins needed for mitosis are made and growth continues.

questions.solution_md: G1, S, G2 with one event each.

questions.stem_md: What is the quiescent stage (G0)? Give two features of cells in it.

answer.model_answer_md: G0 is an **inactive stage that cells enter by leaving G1** when they do not divide further. Cells in G0 stay **metabolically active** but **do not proliferate** unless called on to do so by the needs of the organism; some, like heart cells, remain there, while others can re-enter the cycle.

questions.solution_md: Definition; active but non-dividing; may re-enter.

marking_scheme.step: Exit from G1 into an inactive stage
Metabolically active, not dividing, can re-enter

questions.stem_md: A cell in G2 is described as having 4C DNA but 2n chromosomes. Explain how both statements can be true, and say what happened in S phase to make them so.

answer.model_answer_md: In **S phase** every chromosome is **replicated**, so the DNA doubles from 2C to 4C. The two copies stay attached as **sister chromatids**, held together at a single **centromere**. Chromosomes are counted by their centromeres, so the **number remains 2n** although each chromosome now has two chromatids. The chromatids separate only later, at anaphase of mitosis.

questions.solution_md: Replication makes sister chromatids at one centromere.

marking_scheme.step: Chromatids stay joined at one centromere

questions.stem_md: Describe the cell cycle, giving the phases of interphase with the events of each, the duration of the cycle in human cells, and the quiescent stage.

answer.model_answer_md:
The **cell cycle** is the sequence of events by which a cell duplicates its genome, synthesises other constituents and divides into two. It has **interphase** and the **M phase**. In human cells in culture a cycle takes about **24 hours**, of which the M phase is only about **1 hour**; interphase is therefore over **95 percent** of the cycle.

Interphase has three phases. In **G1** the cell grows and is metabolically active but does not replicate DNA. In **S phase** DNA replicates, its amount doubling from 2C to 4C while the chromosome number stays 2n; in animal cells the centriole duplicates in the cytoplasm. In **G2** proteins are made for mitosis and growth continues.

Cells that do not divide further exit G1 into the **quiescent stage (G0)**: they remain metabolically active but do not proliferate unless called on to do so.

questions.solution_md: Phases and events; timing; G0.

marking_scheme.step: Definition and two parts of the cycle

questions.stem_md: A student looking at a dividing cell sees condensed chromosomes, each of two chromatids, but no nucleolus, no nuclear envelope and no Golgi complex. Spindle fibres are present but the chromosomes are not yet in a line. Which stage is this?
questions.solution_md: By the end of prophase the nucleolus, nuclear envelope, Golgi complex and endoplasmic reticulum have disappeared; alignment on the plate marks metaphase, so the cell is in late prophase — option (d).

questions.stem_md: A cytogeneticist wants to count and examine the shape of the chromosomes in a root-tip squash. At which stage of mitosis are they most suitable for this?

options.text_md: Metaphase, when they are fully condensed on the plate

questions.solution_md: At metaphase the chromosomes are fully condensed and aligned at the metaphase plate, which makes this the best stage for studying their number and morphology — option (b).

questions.stem_md: During metaphase the spindle fibres are attached to each chromosome at

options.text_md: the ends of the chromatid arms

questions.solution_md: Spindle fibres attach to the kinetochores, disc-shaped structures at the centromere of each chromosome — option (c).

questions.stem_md: A fruit-fly cell has 2n = 8. Just after the centromeres split at anaphase of mitosis, how many chromosomes does the whole cell hold?
questions.solution_md: Before the split there were 8 chromosomes of two chromatids each (16 chromatids). Once the centromeres split, each chromatid is a chromosome, so the cell holds 16 — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Garden pea has 2n = 14. How many chromatids are present in a cell at metaphase of mitosis?
questions.solution_md: At metaphase there are 14 chromosomes, each with two chromatids: 14 × 2 = 28 — option (c).

questions.stem_md: Which set of events marks telophase of mitosis?

options.text_md: Centromeres split and chromatids move to the poles
Chromosomes align on the equator with spindle fibres at their kinetochores
Chromosomes condense and the centrosomes move apart
Chromosomes decondense at the poles, and the nuclear envelope, nucleolus, Golgi complex and ER reform

questions.solution_md: Telophase is the reverse of prophase: chromosomes reach the poles and decondense, and the nuclear envelope and the other structures reform — option (d).

questions.stem_md: In a dividing plant cell, the cell plate that grows outwards from the centre eventually becomes

options.text_md: the nuclear envelope of the daughter cells
the plasma membrane of the parent cell
a ring of microtubules that holds the chromosomes
the middle lamella between the two new cells

questions.solution_md: The cell plate represents the middle lamella between the walls of the two daughter cells; wall materials are then laid down on it — option (d).

questions.stem_md: A student examines the liquid endosperm of a tender coconut and finds many nuclei lying in one mass of cytoplasm. This arrangement arises because

options.text_md: the nuclei were produced by meiosis
karyokinesis was repeatedly not followed by cytokinesis
the cell plate formed but failed to meet the cell wall

questions.solution_md: When karyokinesis is not followed by cytokinesis, a multinucleate syncytium results, as in the liquid endosperm of coconut — option (c).

questions.stem_md: The figure shows five stages of mitosis and cytokinesis in a cell with four chromosomes, drawn in scrambled order. In which cell are the chromosomes lined up on the metaphase plate with spindle fibres at their centromeres?
questions.solution_md: Only cell B has its chromosomes in a line at the equator, each attached to spindle fibres from both poles: metaphase. A is telophase, C is cytokinesis, D prophase and E anaphase — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Which of the following is not a function of mitosis in a flowering plant?

options.text_md: Formation of haploid pollen grains from pollen mother cells
Growth in length of a root tip
Replacement of damaged cells in a stem
Production of new cells by the apical meristem

questions.solution_md: Haploid pollen grains arise by meiosis of pollen mother cells; growth, repair and meristem activity are produced by mitosis — option (a).

questions.stem_md: A single-celled alga grows until its cytoplasm is very large for its one nucleus, and then divides. Which role of mitosis does this illustrate?
questions.solution_md: When a cell outgrows the control of its nucleus, division restores the balance between nucleus and cytoplasm; mitosis neither halves the number nor creates variation — option (b).

questions.stem_md: A chemical prevents spindle fibres from forming but does not stop DNA replication or chromosome condensation. After several hours, dividing cells treated with it would pile up with

options.text_md: two complete nuclei but no cell wall
condensed chromosomes that cannot be pulled to the poles, so the cell cannot complete anaphase
chromosomes that have reached the poles and decondensed

questions.solution_md: Without a spindle the chromosomes still condense but cannot be aligned and pulled apart, so the cell is held before anaphase — option (c).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Mitosis gives two daughter nuclei that are genetically identical to the parent nucleus.

**Reason (R):** Homologous chromosomes pair and exchange segments in prophase of mitosis.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: A is true: each chromosome is replicated and its chromatids are shared out equally. R is false: pairing and exchange happen only in prophase I of meiosis — option (c).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A plant cell divides its cytoplasm by forming a cell plate rather than a furrow.

**Reason (R):** A plant cell is enclosed by a rigid cell wall outside its plasma membrane.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: Both statements are true, and the rigid wall prevents the membrane from simply pinching in, so a cell plate grows outwards from the centre instead — option (a).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** At metaphase of mitosis the nuclear envelope is still intact around the chromosomes.

**Reason (R):** Spindle fibres attach to the kinetochores of the chromosomes at metaphase.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: A is false: the nuclear envelope has already disappeared by the end of prophase. R is true: spindle fibres attach to the kinetochores at metaphase — option (d).

questions.stem_md: True or false? Mitosis is called an equational division because each daughter cell receives the same chromosome number as the parent cell.
questions.solution_md: True. A diploid parent cell gives two diploid daughter cells, so the chromosome number is the same.

questions.stem_md: At anaphase of mitosis the ______ of each chromosome splits, and the chromatids move to opposite poles.
questions.solution_md: Centromere.

questions.stem_md: Match each stage of mitosis (column I) with its key event (column II).

match_right.text_md: Centromeres split and chromatids move to opposite poles
Chromosomes condense and the asters move to opposite poles
Chromosomes decondense and the nuclear envelope reforms at each pole
Chromosomes lie on the equatorial plane with spindle fibres at their kinetochores

questions.solution_md: Prophase: condensation and aster movement; metaphase: alignment on the plate; anaphase: centromere splitting and movement of chromatids; telophase: decondensation and reformation of the envelope.

questions.stem_md: In a squash of onion root tip, 350 cells are counted and 28 of them are in some stage of mitosis. What is the mitotic index, in percent?
questions.solution_md: Mitotic index $= \dfrac{28}{350} \times 100 = 8$ percent.

questions.stem_md: Maize has 2n = 20. How many chromatids are present in one cell at the metaphase of mitosis?
questions.solution_md: There are 20 chromosomes, each of two chromatids: $20 \times 2 = 40$.

questions.stem_md: Differentiate between cytokinesis in an animal cell and in a plant cell.

answer.model_answer_md: In an **animal cell** a **furrow** appears in the plasma membrane and deepens **from the edge inwards** until the cytoplasm is cut in two. In a **plant cell**, enclosed by a rigid wall, a **cell plate** forms in the **centre** and grows **outwards** to meet the side walls; it becomes the middle lamella between the new cells.

questions.solution_md: Furrow versus cell plate.

marking_scheme.step: Plant: cell plate, centre to edge, middle lamella

questions.stem_md: Why is metaphase the stage chosen to count chromosomes, and what happens at the next stage to the chromosome numbers?

answer.model_answer_md: At **metaphase** the chromosomes are **fully condensed** and lie in one plane at the **metaphase plate**, so their number and shape are easiest to see. At **anaphase** the **centromeres split** and the chromatids, now chromosomes, move to opposite poles, so the **number of chromosomes in the cell doubles** temporarily.

questions.solution_md: Condensed and aligned; doubling at anaphase.

marking_scheme.step: Metaphase: condensed and aligned on the plate
Anaphase: centromeres split; number doubles in the cell

questions.stem_md: What is a syncytium? Explain how it forms, with one example.

answer.model_answer_md: A **syncytium** is a **multinucleate cell**. It forms when **karyokinesis is not followed by cytokinesis**, so the nuclei produced by repeated nuclear divisions remain in one common cytoplasm. An example is the **liquid endosperm of coconut**.

questions.solution_md: Karyokinesis without cytokinesis.

questions.stem_md: State two ways in which mitosis is important to a multicellular organism, with an example of each.

answer.model_answer_md: Mitosis is responsible for **growth**: a zygote becomes a multicellular body by repeated mitosis. It also **replaces and repairs cells**, as in the skin or the lining of the intestine, and in plants **meristems divide** to add new cells throughout life. In each case the daughter cells are **genetically identical** to the parent.

questions.solution_md: Two roles with examples.

questions.stem_md: Describe the events of prophase of mitosis, including what has disappeared from the cell by its end.

answer.model_answer_md: Prophase follows S and G2 phases. The chromosomal material **condenses**, so each chromosome shows **two chromatids joined at the centromere**. The **centrosome**, which duplicated in S phase, begins to move to **opposite poles** and radiates **microtubules** (asters); these with the spindle fibres form the mitotic apparatus. By the end of prophase the **Golgi complex, endoplasmic reticulum, nucleolus and nuclear envelope have disappeared**.

questions.solution_md: Condensation, centrosomes, disappearance of structures.

marking_scheme.step: Condensation; two chromatids at the centromere
Centrosomes to the poles, asters and spindle

questions.stem_md: A growing cell is dividing by mitosis. State what is meant by the nucleo-cytoplasmic ratio, why it matters, and how mitosis keeps it in balance.

answer.model_answer_md: The **nucleo-cytoplasmic ratio** is the ratio of the volume of the nucleus to that of the cytoplasm. A nucleus can regulate only a limited volume of cytoplasm, so as a cell **grows** the ratio falls and the cell **loses efficient control**. **Mitosis restores the ratio**: each division gives two cells with their own nucleus and a smaller volume of cytoplasm, so the balance between nucleus and cytoplasm is regained.

questions.solution_md: Definition; why; restoration.

marking_scheme.step: Control limited; ratio falls as cell grows

questions.stem_md: Describe the stages of mitosis in an animal cell, with the main events of each stage, and state the significance of mitosis.

answer.model_answer_md:
**Mitosis** is equational division, in which a diploid cell gives two daughter cells with the same chromosome number.

**Prophase:** chromosomes condense, each of two chromatids joined at the centromere; the centrosomes move to the poles and form asters and the spindle; by its end the nucleolus, nuclear envelope, Golgi complex and ER disappear.

**Metaphase:** chromosomes are fully condensed, spindle fibres attach to the kinetochores, and the chromosomes align on the metaphase plate.

**Anaphase:** centromeres split and chromatids move to opposite poles, centromere first.

**Telophase:** chromosomes reach the poles and decondense; the nuclear envelope, nucleolus, Golgi complex and ER reform. Cytokinesis then divides the cytoplasm.

**Significance:** identical daughter cells; growth; restoring the nucleo-cytoplasmic ratio; replacement and repair; meristem activity in plants.

questions.solution_md: Four stages and significance.

questions.stem_md: A student says that all cells divide their cytoplasm in the same way. Evaluate this claim by describing cytokinesis in an animal cell and a plant cell, and by explaining what happens when karyokinesis is not followed by cytokinesis.

answer.model_answer_md:
**The claim is wrong.** Cytokinesis differs in the two kinds of cell.

In an **animal cell** a **furrow** appears in the plasma membrane. It deepens from the edge towards the centre until it meets, cutting the cell into two daughter cells.

A **plant cell** has a **rigid wall** outside the membrane, so it cannot pinch in. Instead a **cell plate** forms in the centre, at the site of the former spindle, and grows **outwards** until it meets the existing side walls. It represents the **middle lamella** between the two new cells, and wall materials are laid down on it.

Sometimes **karyokinesis is not followed by cytokinesis**. The nuclei then stay together in one cytoplasm, forming a **multinucleate syncytium**, as in the **liquid endosperm of coconut**.

questions.solution_md: Furrow, cell plate, syncytium; claim rejected.

marking_scheme.step: Plant cytokinesis by cell plate and why

questions.stem_md: Read the passage and answer the questions that follow.
questions.passage_md:
A student prepares a stained squash of a growing root tip and counts 600 cells under the microscope.

| Stage | Interphase | Prophase | Metaphase | Anaphase | Telophase |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Cells counted | 540 | 30 | 10 | 5 | 15 |

The cells of this root tip complete a cycle in 18 hours, and the cells are at all stages of the cycle.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** (a) Anaphase

**(b)** 10 percent

**(c)** (i) In a population with cells at all stages, the **share of cells in a stage equals the share of the cycle** spent in it. So metaphase lasts the fraction of cells found in it, multiplied by the length of the cycle: $\dfrac{10}{600} \times 18 = 0.3$ hour. Converting hours to minutes gives **18 minutes**.

**OR** (ii) In a population with cells at all stages, the **number of cells in a stage is proportional to the time spent in it**. Prophase lasts **longer** than anaphase, as chromosomes condense and the spindle forms, so more cells are caught in it.

questions.solution_md:
**(a)** In an asynchronous population the fewest cells are found in the shortest stage; anaphase has only 5 cells — option (a).

**(b)** Dividing cells $= 30 + 10 + 5 + 15 = 60$; index $= \dfrac{60}{600} \times 100 = 10$ percent.

**(c)** (i) Share of cells times the cycle.

(ii) Counts proportional to duration.

children.stem_md: Which stage of mitosis is shortest, judging by the counts?
children.solution_md: In an asynchronous population the fewest cells are found in the shortest stage; anaphase has only 5 cells — option (a).

children.stem_md: Calculate the mitotic index of this root tip, in percent.
**Either** (i): Calculate how long, in minutes, a cell spends in metaphase.

answer.model_answer_md: In a population with cells at all stages, the **share of cells in a stage equals the share of the cycle** spent in it. So metaphase lasts the fraction of cells found in it, multiplied by the length of the cycle: $\dfrac{10}{600} \times 18 = 0.3$ hour. Converting hours to minutes gives **18 minutes**.

children.solution_md: Share of cells times the cycle.

marking_scheme.step: Share of cells times cycle length

alternatives.stem_md: **Or** (ii): Explain why more cells are seen in prophase than in anaphase.

answer.model_answer_md: In a population with cells at all stages, the **number of cells in a stage is proportional to the time spent in it**. Prophase lasts **longer** than anaphase, as chromosomes condense and the spindle forms, so more cells are caught in it.

marking_scheme.step: Number in a stage proportional to time

questions.stem_md: An electron micrograph of a meiotic cell shows two homologous chromosomes lying side by side, joined along their length by a ladder-like protein structure. Which substage of prophase I is this?
questions.solution_md: Pairing of homologues (synapsis) with the synaptonemal complex between them is the event of zygotene — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Under the electron microscope, round recombination nodules are seen along tetrads, each made of four chromatids. The cell is in

options.text_md: leptotene, when chromosomes first become visible
diplotene, when the synaptonemal complex dissolves
pachytene, when crossing over takes place
diakinesis, when the nuclear envelope breaks down

questions.solution_md: Tetrads with recombination nodules mark pachytene, the stage of crossing over catalysed by recombinase — option (c).

questions.stem_md: In diplotene the homologous chromosomes of each bivalent seem to pull apart but stay linked at X-shaped points. These points show

options.text_md: the sites where crossing over has taken place
the centromeres, where spindle fibres will attach
the places where the synaptonemal complex is just forming
the points at which DNA replication began

questions.solution_md: The X-shaped chiasmata mark the sites of crossovers between non-sister chromatids — option (a).

questions.stem_md: A meiotic cell shows fully condensed chromosomes with chiasmata at the ends of the arms, an assembled spindle, and no nucleolus or nuclear envelope. Which stage is this?
questions.solution_md: Terminalised chiasmata, full condensation, an assembled spindle and loss of the nucleolus and envelope mark diakinesis, the end of prophase I; in metaphase I the bivalents would already lie on the equator — option (a).

questions.stem_md: A garden pea plant has 2n = 14. After meiosis I, each of the two cells of the dyad holds
questions.solution_md: Homologues separated in anaphase I, so each cell has half the number, 7; the sister chromatids are still joined, so there are 14 chromatids — option (b).

questions.stem_md: How does the arrangement of chromosomes at metaphase I of meiosis differ from that at metaphase of mitosis?

options.text_md: Single chromosomes lie on the equator, each with one chromatid
Chromosomes lie scattered, as no spindle forms in meiosis
Sister chromatids of every chromosome face opposite poles
Bivalents lie on the equator, with the kinetochores of the two homologues facing opposite poles

questions.solution_md: At metaphase I whole bivalents align, and the homologues attach to opposite poles; in mitosis the two chromatids of each chromosome face opposite poles — option (d).

questions.stem_md: In a human meiocyte (2n = 46), how many chromosomes go to each pole at anaphase I, and of how many chromatids is each made?
questions.solution_md: Homologous chromosomes separate, so each pole gets one of each pair: 23. The sister chromatids stay joined, so each has two — option (c).

questions.stem_md: Which statement about the stage between meiosis I and meiosis II is correct?

options.text_md: The chromosomes are replicated again so that each has four chromatids
It is always the longest stage of meiosis
The chromosome number is doubled again in this stage
It is generally short and no DNA replication takes place in it

questions.solution_md: Interkinesis is generally short-lived, and DNA is not replicated in it; only one replication precedes meiosis I — option (d).

questions.stem_md: Maize has 2n = 20. How many chromosomes are present in each cell of the dyad when it reaches metaphase II?
questions.solution_md: The cell has half the diploid number, 10 chromosomes, each of two chromatids — option (a).

questions.stem_md: The figure shows the five substages of prophase I for one pair of homologous chromosomes, in scrambled order. In which cell are the homologues pairing along their length, with no crossing over yet?
questions.solution_md: Cell E shows the two homologues zipped together side by side: zygotene. D is pachytene (with crossing over), A diplotene, B leptotene and C diakinesis — option (b).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Crossing over increases the genetic variability among the gametes formed by meiosis.

**Reason (R):** Crossing over exchanges segments between non-sister chromatids of homologous chromosomes, producing new combinations of genes.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: Both statements are true, and the new gene combinations produced by exchange of segments explain the added variability — option (a).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Sister chromatids separate during anaphase I of meiosis.

**Reason (R):** Homologous chromosomes separate during anaphase I of meiosis.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: A is false: the sister chromatids stay joined at their centromeres in anaphase I and separate only in anaphase II. R is true — option (d).

questions.stem_md: True or false? A bivalent seen at pachytene contains four chromatids.
questions.solution_md: True. A bivalent is a pair of homologous chromosomes, each of two sister chromatids, so it appears as a tetrad of four chromatids.

questions.stem_md: The division of meiosis that reduces the chromosome number to half is meiosis ______.
questions.solution_md: Meiosis I (the reduction division); meiosis II is equational.

questions.stem_md: The two cells formed at the end of meiosis I are together called a ______.
questions.solution_md: Dyad. The four cells after meiosis II form a tetrad.

questions.stem_md: Match each substage of prophase I (column I) with its event (column II).

match_right.text_md: Chromosomes gradually become visible under the light microscope
Synapsis of homologues with the synaptonemal complex
Chiasmata are seen as the synaptonemal complex dissolves

questions.solution_md: Leptotene: chromosomes become visible; zygotene: synapsis; pachytene: crossing over at the nodules; diplotene: chiasmata appear as the complex dissolves.

questions.stem_md: A flower’s anther must release 2000 pollen grains. Each pollen mother cell gives four pollen grains by meiosis. How many pollen mother cells are needed?
questions.solution_md: $\dfrac{2000}{4} = 500$ pollen mother cells.

questions.stem_md: A section of a testis holds 120 meiocytes, each of which completes meiosis and produces four haploid cells. How many haploid cells result?
questions.solution_md: $4 \times 120 = 480$ haploid cells.

questions.stem_md: What is interkinesis? State two of its features.

answer.model_answer_md: **Interkinesis** is the stage between meiosis I and meiosis II. It is **generally short-lived**, and **no DNA replication takes place** in it, so the chromosomes are not copied again before the second division.

questions.stem_md: What is crossing over? State where and in which stage it occurs.

answer.model_answer_md: **Crossing over** is the **exchange of segments between non-sister chromatids** of homologous chromosomes. It takes place in **pachytene** of prophase I, at **recombination nodules**, and is catalysed by the enzyme **recombinase**. It leads to **recombination** of genes.

questions.stem_md: Why is meiosis I called the reduction division while meiosis II is called equational?

answer.model_answer_md: In **meiosis I** homologous chromosomes separate, so each of the two cells receives **half the chromosome number**: the number is **reduced**. In **meiosis II** the sister chromatids separate, as in mitosis, so each cell keeps the **same chromosome number** it started with: the division is **equational**.

marking_scheme.step: Meiosis I: homologues separate; number halved
Meiosis II: chromatids separate; number unchanged

questions.stem_md: Describe what happens to the homologous chromosomes in zygotene, pachytene and diplotene of prophase I.

answer.model_answer_md: In **zygotene** homologous chromosomes **pair** (synapsis) along their length, aided by the **synaptonemal complex**, forming bivalents. In **pachytene** each bivalent shows **four chromatids** (a tetrad) and **crossing over** occurs between non-sister chromatids at recombination nodules. In **diplotene** the complex dissolves and the homologues **separate except at the chiasmata**, the X-shaped sites of crossing over.

questions.solution_md: Pairing; crossing over; chiasmata.

questions.stem_md: Compare what separates, and what each pole receives, in anaphase I and anaphase II of meiosis.

answer.model_answer_md: In **anaphase I** the **homologous chromosomes** of each bivalent separate, but **sister chromatids stay joined** at the centromeres; each pole receives **half the chromosome number**, each chromosome of two chromatids. In **anaphase II** the **centromeres split** and the **sister chromatids** move to opposite poles, so each pole receives single-chromatid chromosomes, as in mitosis.

marking_scheme.step: Anaphase I: homologues separate; chromatids stay joined
Anaphase II: centromere splits; chromatids separate

questions.stem_md: Explain two ways in which meiosis is significant for sexually reproducing organisms.

answer.model_answer_md: Meiosis **halves the chromosome number** in gametes, so that **fusion of two haploid gametes** restores the diploid number; without it the number would **double every generation**. It also **increases genetic variability**, through **crossing over** and the separation of homologues, giving a population variations that are very important for **evolution**.

questions.solution_md: Constant chromosome number; variability.

marking_scheme.step: Halving keeps the number constant across generations

questions.stem_md: Describe the stages of meiosis I, including the substages of prophase I, and say what separates at the end of this division.

answer.model_answer_md:
**Meiosis I** follows replication of the chromosomes into sister chromatids in S phase.

**Prophase I** has five substages. **Leptotene:** chromosomes become visible. **Zygotene:** homologues pair (synapsis) with the synaptonemal complex, forming bivalents. **Pachytene:** tetrads of four chromatids; crossing over at recombination nodules. **Diplotene:** the complex dissolves and homologues separate except at chiasmata. **Diakinesis:** chiasmata terminalise, chromosomes fully condensed, spindle assembles, nucleolus and envelope disappear.

**Metaphase I:** bivalents lie on the equator, homologues attached to opposite poles. **Anaphase I:** homologous chromosomes separate; sister chromatids stay joined. **Telophase I:** envelope and nucleolus reappear; cytokinesis gives a dyad of haploid cells.

questions.solution_md: Prophase I substages; metaphase I to telophase I.

questions.stem_md: A student confuses mitosis and meiosis. Write five differences between them in a table, and state one similarity.

answer.model_answer_md:
| Feature | Mitosis | Meiosis |
|---|---|---|
| Cells that divide | Somatic cells, meristems | Meiocytes of reproductive organs |
| Divisions per DNA replication | One | Two |
| Pairing of homologues; crossing over | Absent | Present in prophase I |
| Daughter cells | Two, diploid, identical | Four, haploid, genetically different |
| Role | Growth, repair, replacement | Gamete formation; constant chromosome number; variability |

**Similarity:** both are preceded by one round of DNA replication in S phase and both involve a spindle, with the chromatids separating at anaphase of mitosis and of meiosis II.

questions.solution_md: Five differences and one similarity.

questions.stem_md: Prophase I of meiosis is long and complex. Describe its five substages in order, mentioning the key event of each and the term for the structures formed by pairing.

answer.model_answer_md:
Prophase I is prolonged and has five substages.

**Leptotene:** the chromosomes gradually become visible under the light microscope and compaction continues.

**Zygotene:** homologous chromosomes start pairing and aligning (**synapsis**), aided by the synaptonemal complex; the paired chromosomes are called **bivalents** or tetrads.

**Pachytene:** bivalents clearly appear as tetrads of four chromatids; **crossing over** between non-sister chromatids occurs at recombination nodules, catalysed by recombinase.

**Diplotene:** the synaptonemal complex dissolves and the homologues separate except at the **chiasmata**, the sites of crossing over.

**Diakinesis:** chiasmata terminalise, chromosomes are fully condensed, the spindle assembles, and the nucleolus and nuclear envelope disappear.

questions.solution_md: Five substages in order.

A student places one yeast cell in a nutrient medium and counts cells at intervals. Each cell divides by mitosis once every 90 minutes, and none die.

| Time (minutes) | 0 | 90 | 180 | 270 | 360 | 450 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Number of cells | 1 | 2 | 4 | 8 | 16 | 32 |

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** (c) The number of cells doubles in each cycle of 90 minutes

**(b)** 128

**(c)** (i) **Interphase** makes up most of the cycle, over **95 percent** in human cells, while the M phase takes only about an hour. In interphase the cell is **metabolically active**: it **grows** (G1 and G2), **replicates its DNA** (S phase) and makes the proteins needed for mitosis.

**OR** (ii) Each cell in the population **replicates its DNA and divides by mitosis into two cells**, so **every cell present** gives two daughters in the next cycle. The increase therefore depends on the number of cells already present, and the number **doubles**.

**(b)** $\dfrac{630}{90} = 7$ cycles, and $2^{7} = 128$ cells.

**(c)** (i) Interphase and its events.

(ii) Every cell divides into two.

questions.stem_md: In a root-tip squash, 400 cells are counted and 36 of them are dividing. Define the mitotic index, calculate it for this preparation, and say what a much higher index in another tissue would suggest.

answer.model_answer_md: The **mitotic index** is the percentage of cells in a sample that are in the M phase (dividing). Here it is $\dfrac{36}{400} \times 100 = 9$ percent. A **much higher index** would suggest a tissue in which **cells are dividing actively**, such as a growing meristem, since a larger share of its cells is caught in mitosis at any moment.
